title: More than $3m spent on government merch, including condoms and lollies
text:
The Albanese government has launched a clampdown on taxpayer-funded merchandise in a bid to rein in the millions of dollars spent on promotional knick-knacks.

Stress balls, condoms, lollies, tote bags, pens and beanies were among thousands of branded or promotional products bought by federal entities in the past financial year.

The total cost across a range of government departments, agencies, independent statutory authorities, regulators and other entities came in at more than $3.4 million.

But under a new edict that came into effect from July, the government has banned agencies from using taxpayer funds to purchase promotional merchandise unless they seek approval.

Coalition outlines costings for cuts Angus Taylor publishes fresh costings for proposed cuts to Labor's climate and housing policies.

There are some exemptions, such as if items are sold for profit or if they are considered critical to the government's policy objectives.

The policy, which was part of this year's budget, mandates that agencies must also publicly report details of their merchandise spend in their annual reports.

"The Department of Finance has issued guidance to agencies to support implementation of the government's policy," a government spokesperson told the ABC.

What the departments spent

The Department of Defence was among the biggest spenders in 2025–26, putting more than $1.4 million towards merchandise, according to figures provided to the Senate.

This included gifts for foreign militaries and dignitaries, as well as items for recruitment activities, employment expos and base open days.

A Defence spokesperson said officials must ensure spending on merchandise represented an efficient, effective, economic and ethical use of public resources.

Another $383,000 was also spent at the health department, which included 40,000 condoms in an initiative aimed at preventing sexually transmitted infections.

Branded condom wallets were procured for an STI prevention campaign. (Supplied)

It also purchased 7,000 campaign-branded "condom wallets".

Among the other items the department bought were 5,000 stress balls, 5,000 mints packs, and 220 yo-yos — all with anti-vaping messages.

A department spokesperson defended its spend on merchandise, saying it was procured in limited circumstances for public health campaigns or strategies.

"Evaluation of these campaigns consistently show they are highly engaging, are well recognised by their target audiences and meet the campaign objectives," they said.

"Merchandise plays an important role in this.

"When used, merchandise carries important health messages and information, such as vaccine schedules, reminders of the importance of STI testing and scheduling, and strategies to assist in how to quit vaping and smoking."

Fewer 'branded generic keepsakes'

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) also incurred $176,000 in merchandise costs last financial year, with most of it aimed at spruiking this year's census.

This included census-themed beanies, mini AFL footballs, socks, reusable shopping bags, pencils, pens and "I heart census" button badge pins.

An ABS spokesperson said its agency had not purchased any further promotional material since the government's new merchandise policy came into effect.

Public servants repay credit card charges Some public servants were required to repay thousands of dollars in inadvertent charges on their work credit cards, including food delivery orders, in the past financial year.

"Census merchandise was used at community events, information hubs, during remote community engagement activities and to support the enumeration of people experiencing homelessness," they said.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) spent more than $251,000, with a spokesperson saying it uses "standardised promotional material" for career expos and fairs.

The spokesperson also said it was "reasonable to expect" some of its reported expenditure on merchandise was used to purchase items from the AFP Legacy Shop.

"The AFP has formal governance on the acquisition of merchandise and has recently tightened this governance further to ensure a greater proportion of our merchandise has an educational element, rather than branded generic keepsakes," they said.

title: Courtney Barnett's songs aren't just about Courtney Barnett
text:
Courtney Barnett is in her late-30s, over a decade into an incredibly successful music career, and past the point of being Australia's next big thing: she arrived a while ago.

Where some artists fear maturity might dull their edge, Barnett recognises how experience works in her favour.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

While making her latest album, Creature Of Habit, disjointed recording sessions and writer's block had the singer-songwriter feeling a little unstable. But this wasn't her first time at the big dance.

"There were moments where I thought it would never get finished," she says.

"It kind of comes in waves. I think that's just the creative process for me: it's ups and downs. I said to myself, 'I've been here before. I've made a few albums, and I've felt this feeling. I'm just going to trust that hopefully I'll pass whatever the difficult moment is and just get on with it.'"

Old habits die

Spoiler: it did pass, resulting in yet another remarkable collection of songs in which Barnett captures our insecurities and reflects them with startling clarity.

That's long been one of her great strengths as a songwriter. The details in a Courtney Barnett song often belong to her, but the feelings somehow belong to everybody.

Review: Courtney Barnett — Creature of Habit The Melbourne songwriter's new album feels like a welcome return to guitar-bass-drums form.

"I know I got a sensitive heart, I'm always picking it apart when I throw it to the vultures. They don't want it either, probably too sincere," she sings on Sugar Plum, a highlight from Creature Of Habit.

Barnett won audiences over from the outset with sharply observed stories about the messy process of trying to figure out life. Her songs often felt intensely personal, but left enough room for listeners to find themselves inside them.

When the young, shy artist was thrust into the spotlight following the success of her early EPs, those innermost thoughts suddenly became open to scrutiny. Seeing her work picked apart by strangers was unsettling.

These days, she's more accustomed to it.

"It kind of adds up, time and experience and all those things … I just feel a little more comfortable doing what I do," Barnett says about her current standing.

While she feels the impact of years in the game, she still finds it a challenge to pinpoint what exactly has changed.

"I feel like I've learned a lot a lot of small but important lessons, but sometimes I don't quite know how to articulate them. One of them is just learning how to trust myself a bit more.

"In the past, I would often spiral into this self-doubt, which just doesn't feel very productive or enjoyable.

"Even just facing a difficult moment and just working through it, something that sounds kind of simple; it was hard to trust in that process.

"Sometimes you got to fake it till you make it. You've got to convince yourself that you 100 per cent know what you're doing."

Start somewhere

While experience helped, Barnett also benefited from coming back to her discipline with fresh eyes.

Making the 2023 instrumental album End of the Day — the soundtrack to the Anonymous Club documentary about her life on the road — gave her a chance to work in a different realm.

"When I started working on it, I was just kind of learning how to write again because I hadn't written a song for a little while," she says. "So, it felt in a way that I was kind of beginning again.

"I was doing a lot of free writing, trying not to go into writing with any kind of intention or idea. I was kind of just trying to understand what was rattling around in my head as unfiltered as humanly possible.

"I guess a lot of my writing is kind of like that. Then it shows me something and then I kind of piece a narrative or an idea together. I guess it was just a thing circling in my head."

Loading Instagram content

Condensing swirling thoughts into compact and compelling cuts of relatable indie rock is not easy on a technical level. Making sense of that flood of thoughts can be just as challenging.

What's worse, there's not really anywhere to hide when you're bleeding onto the page.

"It can be confronting, because you're face to face with yourself and holding a mirror up to yourself and sometimes you see things that you don't like," Barnett says.

"I was exploring parts of my personality or just parts of my world or life. I guess that kind of plays into the album title.

"I was looking at parts of myself that I didn't really like or that I wanted to change or wanted to work on, and kind of gently and kindly doing that work or making those subtle changes."

The You and the I

In many of her best songs, Barnett tells stories about her own life. A medical incident in Avant Gardener, a trip to an open home she can't afford in Depreston, the general suburban malaise of Rae Street. But the inward focus is not always intentional.

Listen to the Courtney Barnett J Files Courtney Barnett is one of the most important songwriters of a generation - a self-made success who renewed a global appetite for music that finds meaning in the mundane.

"I think that sometimes when I do look out, or write something for someone else, or to someone else, it often makes its way back around to me somehow," she says.

"Whether that's putting myself in someone's shoes or finding some kind of level of connection or empathy or something. I don't know. But I often end up talking to myself in a weird roundabout way."

And if you see yourself in Barnett's songs, you're right. If you reckon she's singing about you, she's not going to argue.

"The 'you' and the 'me' and the 'I'… it's kind of interchangeable," she says.

"In some songs, I might be addressing multiple people or things in my head, but it might sound like it's to just one person."

Of course, the song and its intent don't necessarily belong to its creator. Perhaps music's most magical power is allowing us to interpret it how we feel, and project our own emotions and life onto it.

"It's why I don't like over explaining meanings of songs, I don't always find it necessary," Barnett says.

"I love learning what old songs are about and the story that is behind some old classic song, but also, it's nice that we get to project our own stuff onto music. I think that's really beautiful."

Making connections with those who see themselves in her songs brings the purpose of her endeavours into sharpest focus.

"I was just thinking of moments in my life where someone has come up to me and said exactly that. They've been the moments where I have really truly felt that connection. I'm really grateful for that," she says.

"I think it's sometimes it's so hard to know… you're just sitting in your room making music and then it goes on the internet and there's comments and all that stuff…

"But sometimes it doesn't really connect until a human says that or I play a show and I see people singing along or having an emotional moment. That's extremely powerful. I'm really grateful for those moments."

Courtney Barnett plays Brisbane on Wednesday before shows in Sydney and Melbourne on Friday and Saturday.

Creature Of Habit is out now.

title: More than 3,000 deaths in Indonesia linked to fire pollution, report says
text:
Pollution from smoke emitted by months of wildfires across Indonesia caused an estimated 3,560 deaths in the vast South-East Asian archipelago in September, according to a new study.

The same month, about 57.8 million people in Indonesia were inhaling unhealthy-to-hazardous air, said the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank.

"Worsening air quality due to forest and land fires in Indonesia pushed the estimated death toll to 3,560 cases in September 2026, a twofold increase from the August estimate," said a CREA statement on Thursday.

The CREA study estimated the number of deaths brought about by PM2.5 pollution in the short-term, meaning a matter of days.

PM2.5 particles are small enough to penetrate the lungs or bloodstream and the World Health Organization has linked exposure to a higher risk of illness and premature death.

Most estimated deaths occurred on Indonesia's part of Borneo island as well as on Java and Sumatra islands and in the country's east, said the report.

Wildfires affected the peatland area, in Ketapang, West Kalimantan province. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

The researchers also looked at non-fire pollution from urban power generation, industry and transportation, and found it had caused a further 1,750 deaths in September for a total of 5,310 in the country of about 290 million people.

"In September alone, exposure levels breached the WHO annual PM2.5 threshold … by over seven times nationally, 10 times in Sumatra, and an alarming 24 times in Kalimantan" in Borneo, said the report.

More than 330,000 cases of acute respiratory infection have been recorded countrywide.

'Predictable and avoidable'

Gripped by drought worsened by the El Niño weather phenomenon, Indonesia has for months battled wildfires that deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas says have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.

The government has not confirmed or rejected the number.

Volunteer firefighters assisted with wildfires in an affected peatland area, in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

The resulting haze has sent pollution levels soaring as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor, clouding Indonesia's ties with its neighbours.

Experts say the wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often by timber, palm oil or mining companies.

For the island of Java, the most populated and home to the capital Jakarta, the CREA report said between 73 and 80 per cent of air pollution deaths, a total of 1,530 in September, were attributed to non-fire sources such as industry, vehicle emissions, and waste burning.

"These figures underscore the stark reality that non-fire air pollution sources are as dangerous as smoke from burning forests and peatlands," it said.

In the report, the CEO of Landscape Indonesia consultancy, Agus Sari, pointed to the government's "weak preparedness" for what he described as a "predictable and avoidable" disaster.

Agus pointed to budget cuts hampering the efforts of the BNPB national disaster management agency.

"Indonesia should be able to prepare for what is going to happen. The fact that we are not prepared at all is purely a matter of lacking the will," Agus said.

The CREA report argues the government needs to shift from a wildfire response to the restoration of peatlands left fire-prone by extensive draining.

"This step must be accompanied by firm law enforcement against illegal land clearing through burning, as well as strengthened legal accountability for concession holders to prevent damage," it said.

AFP

title: Ferrari fastest as Verstappen says Kiwi rival should 'act a little smarter'
text:
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fastest in both practice sessions for a Mexico City Grand Prix set to crown 20-year-old Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli as Formula 1's youngest champion.

Antonelli missed Thursday's media day to recover from a viral illness, but the Italian was second on the time sheets in the first session and fourth in the later one at the capital's high-altitude Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title in Mexico The Mexico City Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Kimi Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli is 123 points clear of teammate George Russell at the top and needs only two more points, a ninth place, to be sure of the title while the Briton has to win on Sunday to stay mathematically in the game with four rounds remaining.

Leclerc, who was also fastest in both Friday sessions in Texas last week before Antonelli won, produced a best effort of 1:17.827 in the second practice, when the times were much closer, after going top in the first by 0.659 with a lap of 1:18.128.

"Overall, our performance looks quite all right, but we still need to work on some of our limiting factors. It was quite tricky on track today, as the surface was slippery," Leclerc said.

McLaren's reigning world champion and last year's winner, Lando Norris, was second fastest in the later session, 0.103 slower, with Russell third.

Leclerc's teammate and seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, a two-time winner in Mexico, stopped on track and triggered a virtual safety car with half an hour remaining. "I lost all power," Hamilton said.

Red flags were shown and the session halted after Red Bull's Max Verstappen, a five-time winner in Mexico, and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, a former teammate, made contact with 47 minutes to go, leaving debris from the Dutch driver's car on the track.

"He literally just drove into me. Every weekend," Lawson said over the radio.

Verstappen hit back at the New Zealander, whose place has yet to be confirmed for next year.

"At the end of the day, it is not going to change my weekend, but if I were him I would act a little smarter. And when you're fighting for your seat, it's not very smart behaviour," he said.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Mexico City Grand Prix on Monday, November 2, from 5:30am AEDT.

title: Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising. Here's how to protect yourself
text:
It starts as a small, painless lump on the skin that is easy to ignore.

But under the seemingly innocuous lump, flesh-eating bacteria are burrowing through fat and muscle.

Warning: Readers are advised that this article includes an image of an open wound.

The skin over the lump then dies, turns black and eventually becomes an open sore that, if untreated, grows.

This is a typical case of Buruli ulcer, a condition that until recently was primarily found in West Africa.

Victoria is now considered the Buruli ulcer centre of the world, with a record 426 confirmed cases last year.

Buruli ulcer is typically acquired in summer and autumn.

It is endemic in the Mornington Peninsula, Bellarine Peninsula, Geelong and some Melbourne suburbs.

It is also found in other parts of Australia: pockets of coastal Queensland, where it is sometimes called Daintree ulcer, and around Darwin.

Most recently, cases have popped up on the New South Wales south coast around Batemans Bay.

Visitors to these popular tourism areas might unknowingly get infected, go home and, months later, develop a Buruli ulcer where local doctors may not be aware of the condition.

So, coming into summer holidays, how can you protect yourself from the disease?

What causes Buruli ulcer?

Buruli ulcer is caused by the microbe Mycobacterium ulcerans.

It can be transmitted to humans via mosquitoes, so ulcers usually appear in areas near bites, such as on arms and legs.

Loading...

Once in the skin, the bacteria secrete a cocktail of molecules that numb the area, slowly kill surrounding tissues and suppress the immune system.

"These things make it quite an impressive pathogen, and often, it's been there for a while before people actually know they've got it," Daniel O'Brien, an infectious diseases physician at Barwon Health in Geelong and Royal Melbourne Hospital, says.

The progression of lump to ulcer happens in about 90 per cent of Buruli ulcer cases he sees.

In less than 1 per cent of cases, the bacteria reach bone.

How is Buruli ulcer diagnosed and treated?

Buruli ulcer advances so slowly that the first symptoms usually are not noticed until five or six months after the infection.

It is diagnosed by sending a swab off for PCR testing to see whether the ulcer contains M. ulcerans bacteria.

Treatment starts with a six-to-eight-week course of antibiotics, but the drugs themselves can be problematic. They interact with many other medications and produce side effects so awful that about 20 per cent of patients cannot finish the whole course.

M. ulcerans infections can start off looking like nasty spider bites that do not heal, Dr O'Brien says, but eventually turn into ulcers. (Supplied)

Dr O'Brien is leading a team trialling a new antibiotic that can be taken over just 10 days, which he says is less harsh on the body, yet still effective against M. ulcerans.

For most people, antibiotics will be enough, but if there is too much tissue damage or the wound is not healing properly, surgery is needed.

Even with treatment and good wound care, it can take months — even a year — for an ulcer to fully heal.

Dr O'Brien says outcomes for patients are generally better if the ulcer is diagnosed early.

For that reason, he recommends getting a health practitioner to look at any suspicious lumps sooner rather than later, especially if you live or holidayed in an area known to have the bacterium, and to specifically ask about Buruli ulcer.

How can I protect myself from Buruli ulcer?

While Buruli ulcer prevalence is rising, Dr O'Brien says it is important to remember that the disease is still uncommon in humans.

" If you protect yourself from the environment … you really minimise your risk of acquisition. "

While mosquitoes are a main source of Buruli ulcers, they are not the only one.

Brushtail and ringtail possums are also known to get infected, and can develop nasty ulcers on their paws, face and tail.

A 2025 study found that analysing the poo of possums could help predict regions where Buruli ulcer might crop up next, with human cases usually appearing up to three years after the first positive possum poo test.

That is because possums shed the bacteria in droppings, introducing it to the soil, which can then get into cuts in our skin.

Dr O'Brien's advice is to:

cover up as much as possible

wear mosquito repellent on exposed skin

cover any wounds while handling soil, and if you injure yourself, wash it immediately with soap and water, then apply antiseptic

avoid handling sick or injured possums

A recent study found reducing mosquito numbers in Buruli ulcer areas also lowered human case numbers, so it is a good idea to tip out standing water where mosquitoes breed and put out mosquito traps.

It is also important to note that research shows not all possums in Buruli-endemic areas carry the bacteria, and it is illegal to trap, relocate or cull possums without a licence.

And, in good news for ringtails and bushies, an edible possum vaccine in the works could help reduce infections and ulcers in the future.

Hear more about Buruli ulcer on Outbreaks, a special series on Science Friction.

title: Bunnings shelves Halloween straitjacket costume after criticism
text:
Bunnings has removed a straitjacket costume from its online marketplace as mental health advocates urge retailers to stop selling Halloween outfits that portray people with mental illness as "insane".

The costume, listed on Bunnings Marketplace, was a straitjacket with arm ties and the words "Property of the county mental institution — approach with caution!" printed on the back.

SANE Australia, a non-profit organisation for people with complex mental health issues, said it was unacceptable for corporations to publicly support mental health causes while profiting from products that reinforce stigma.

"The time has well and truly come for us to stop turning a blind eye to these kinds of tropes in the community," CEO Rachel Green told ABC Victoria Statewide Drive.

" You wouldn't see people buying and wearing a cancer patient costume, for example. So why is a costume dressing up as someone with a mental illness considered acceptable? "

Rachel Green says it's unacceptable for businesses to publicly support mental health while profiting from products that reinforce stigma. (Supplied: SANE Australia)

Sandy Jeffs, a SANE ambassador and author who lives with schizophrenia and was a patient at Melbourne's former Larundel Psychiatric Hospital, said the costumes were insulting and "downright mad-shaming".

"Halloween, it's fun for people, but I suppose it's when it goes to negative tropes like introducing straitjackets as a costume — it goes into a dark place," she said.

"They're there to laugh at, to make fun of, to really demonise a whole cohort of people who don't deserve to be demonised or to be laughed at and shamed.

" We're just ordinary people with a very extraordinary illness … dealing with the stigma that surrounds these conditions every day. "

If you or anyone you know needs help: Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Headspace on 1800 650 890

When contacted by the ABC, a spokesperson for Bunnings said the item had since been removed from sale.

"We understand the concerns raised, and once the listing was brought to our attention, it was removed from Bunnings Marketplace," a spokesperson said.

The same costume is available for sale at Kmart, which, like Bunnings, is owned by Wesfarmers, as well as at Dick Smith, Amazon and a number of smaller costume stores.

The ABC has contacted Wesfarmers for comment.

Not the first time

It's not the first time SANE has called out retailers for selling costumes it considers stigmatising.

SANE said a social media campaign in 2024 prompted Big W to remove Halloween costumes from sale.

Ms Green said Spotlight was among the retailers that quickly pulled the costume at the time, but had since made it available for sale again.

The costume remained available on the Spotlight website on Saturday. (Supplied: Spotlight)

She said the costumes mattered for families dealing with serious mental illness.

"It does matter for the family who've got a 25-year-old who's got early signs of psychosis and is really struggling and needs to have that support wrapped around them," Ms Green said.

"How are they going to feel with people walking around on Saturday dressed in a costume that's a caricature of a bygone era."

The ABC has contacted Spotlight for comment.

title: Person in life-threatening condition with meningococcal B infection
text:
An adult is on life support in an Adelaide hospital with invasive meningococcal infection.

SA has had 22 cases of meningococcal disease reported this year, up from 13 at the same time in 2025.

The fast-progressing disease prompted authorities to call for greater uptake of the Meningococcal B vaccine.

"I think at the moment we have roughly 50 per cent of eligible people in our state who are actually vaccinated and covered for meningococcal B," Health Minister Blair Boyer said.

The Meningococcal B vaccine is free for South Australian children aged six weeks to 12 months, and school students in Year 10.

"The kids most at risk are the young children," Chief Public Health Officer Nicola Spurrier said.

" The other highest risk group is 15 to 20-year-olds, and that's why we have the school-based program. "

Very close contact required for transmission

Professor Spurrier said SA Health had already performed contact tracing and the risk to the wider population from the infected person was low.

Seven close contacts have been identified to receive clearance antibiotics to prevent further transmission.

"That means they've had the antibiotics, it reduces that carriage of the bacteria in the back of the nose and throat and therefore can't be passed on to anyone else," Professor Spurrier said.

How Australia could be at risk of a meningitis outbreak A growing outbreak of meningococcal B and meningitis has killed two in the UK. Here's why Brisbane's infectious disease professor is worried.

Invasive meningococcal disease is caused by an infection with Neisseria meningitidis bacteria, of which there are 13 known types. Around a tenth of the population harmlessly carries the bacteria in their nose and throat where it causes no harm.

However, the pathogen can be transmitted to others at times of prolonged or very close contact — often by living in the same household — and spread to the bloodstream and brain.

Symptoms include skin rash, headache, fever, vomiting, neck stiffness and discomfort when looking at lights. These can progress to confusion and shock. Symptoms require urgent medical attention as death can occur within 24 hours. According to SA Health, up to 10 per cent of infected people can die, even with rapid treatment.

title: Fancied Melbourne Cup horse Defiantly ruled out by vets
text:
One of the leading international challengers for the Melbourne Cup, Defiantly, has been ruled out of the race after failing a vet's inspection on Saturday.

The Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, which had been a long-time favourite for the race, had won the Group Two Prix Kergorlay race over 3,000m at Deauville in France.

Defiantly was in quarantine at Werribee after arriving in Australia, and had failed an initial inspection on Thursday.

The horse was re-examined on Saturday morning.

"In the opinion of the veterinarians, Defiantly remains unsuitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup and has been withdrawn from the race by order of the stewards acting on veterinary advice," Racing Victoria said in a statement.

Williams eyes Melbourne Cup success Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Craig Williams hopes racing's version of a blind date will quickly evolve into a successful partnership as he eyes further glory in the race that stops a nation.

Defiantly's absence makes it likely that another Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, Kizlyar, will take its place in the field.

Two other international chances in the race, Enfjaar and Wine Dark Sea, had also failed initial assessments, but they passed inspection on Saturday and are approved to accept their spots in Tuesday's race.

Defiantly is the second international ruled out of this year's Melbourne Cup. Japanese entry Stinger Glass was ruled out after CT and PET scans showed the horse was at heightened risk of injury.

The Ciaron Maher-trained Saint George, who was runner-up in the Caulfield Cup a fortnight ago, before coming fifth in the Cox Plate last weekend, was also removed from the race after CT scans showed he was at heightened risk of injury.

The scans and vet inspections are part of veterinary protocols to ensure each horse is suitable to accept a place in the final field.

The field will be finalised at 4:30pm AEDT, followed by the Melbourne Cup draw an hour later.

ABC

title: New chapter begins in Fremantle as Walyalup Bridge set to open
text:
It's been 70 years since Jan Middleton and her two colleagues survived a dramatic plunge off the old Fremantle Traffic Bridge, their car plummeting 10 metres to land on its roof.

It was 1956 and Ms Middleton, then 22, was giving her co-worker, Barbara Shimmon, a driving lesson during their lunch break.

Their colleague Thelma Davies decided to tag along, eating her lunch in the back seat as the trio headed towards Fremantle from Mosman Park.

"As we approached the bridge, it was sprinkling rain and we hit a bit of wet oil in the road," Ms Middleton said.

Ms Middleton's family included a picture of the flipped car in a photo book documenting her life. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"We did two complete circles in the middle of the road, slewed across [and] hit one of the cement pillars."

Ms Middleton said the car flipped backwards off the bridge.

"We teetered on the side before over we went and landed on the hood," she said.

"I recall feeling disappointed, because I knew I was going to die.

"After that I gave up teaching friends to drive."

Jan Middleton was teaching her colleague how to drive when their car skidded off the bridge (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Astonishingly, all three women escaped the wreck without serious injury.

"For the next week to go to work, we all took cushions because our bones were bruised, but apart from that, we were fine," Ms Middleton said.

Newspaper clippings from the time show the car flipped upside down. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

New chapter for bridge

Now aged 92, Ms Middleton will be among the first to walk across the new Fremantle Traffic Bridge, officially named Walyalup Bridge, when it opens on Sunday, four months ahead of schedule.

The 86-year-old wooden bridge was closed in February to allow for the construction of the new bridge, which was expected to take 12 months.

But while the project is ahead of schedule, the final price tag has more than doubled from the initial cost announced in 2021 of $230 million, now coming in at $596m.

The new Fremantle Traffic Bridge is a joint state and federal government project. (Supplied: WA government)

Traffic authorities warned of potentially significant delays, prompting the government to consider limiting truck movements across the Stirling Bridge at peak hour to limit traffic congestion.

Authorities implemented several changes to the local transport network to accommodate the closure, including additional train and bus services, more free parking bays for SmartRider users and increased monitoring of traffic via CCTV.

The new, 500-metre bridge has the same number of traffic lanes but wider pedestrian paths and a higher clearance for boats and is the first "extradosed" bridge to be built in Australia, combining both cantilevers and cable stay supports.

The second Fremantle Traffic Bridge, which was recently demolished, being built in the mid 1930s. (Supplied: State Library Western Australia)

Walyalup Bridge is the third Fremantle Traffic Bridge. The first was built by convicts in the mid 1800s and the second opened in 1939.

title: Learning Auslan a 'life skill' for children
text:
Inside a classroom in regional Western Australia, students are so quiet they could hear a pin drop.

The lack of audible chatter is not a reflection of the communication taking place.

The silence is the sound of focus and concentration while learning a language.

Angela Linfitt provides resources for Beverley District High's classes. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Students are taking part in Auslan classes, a program that has fast become the favourite subject of students at Beverley District High School, 120 kilometres east of Perth.

Students from pre-primary to year 8 take part in up to two Auslan classes a week under the guidance of hearing teacher Isabel Freeman.

And they are not alone, with statistics from the Department of Education showing nearly 130 public schools in the state now teach Auslan.

Four years of learning

Ms Freeman began sharing her Auslan knowledge by chance while working at the school as a secondary English and HASS teacher.

"We had a non-verbal student at the school, and I was teaching her Auslan," she said.

"And when the Italian teacher retired, because Italian was our Language Other Than English, the school asked me if I would like to teach Auslan."

Isabel Freeman has been teaching Auslan at Beverley District High School for four years. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Ms Freeman said that as a hearing Auslan teacher, the consultation of her Auslan mentor and qualified Deaf teacher Angela Linfitt meant teaching was culturally appropriate and considered.

"It makes it more authentic," she said.

Ms Linfitt has mentored Ms Freeman throughout her Auslan teaching, and said the expansion of Auslan in schools created more career opportunities for deaf professionals.

Angela Linfitt has helped shape the Beverley District High School Auslan program. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

"It's critical [to have deaf mentoring] because deaf people are professionals, they are specialists of their own language," Ms Linfitt said.

"It's really important to have [deaf people] involved in the program to make sure it's being taught correctly."

In WA, school-based Auslan teachers are required to hold a teacher's registration and be trained in Auslan, requirements Ms Linfitt said could rule out members of the deaf community.

"Unfortunately there isn't enough funding at the moment for deaf people to be involved in those roles," she said.

"It can be very difficult to go to university for a deaf person, they face many barriers.

"We need additional support to access services and get through that system."

Creating an inclusive environment

Bethel Fraser says she enjoys sharing the language with others. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Student Bethel Fraser sits front and centre during her Auslan class, eagerly repeating back words and phrases.

She said she enjoyed sharing her skills with others.

"In Auslan we can teach other people around us so that soon everybody knows Auslan so we can communicate with the deaf," she said.

There is one child enrolled at the school with a diagnosed hearing impairment.

Wendy Norris has seen Auslan skills applied outside the classroom. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Beverley District High School principal Wendy Norris, who joined the school earlier this year, said she was amazed at how engaged students were with the program.

"It allows our students to be inclusive in the community as well," she said.

"It's not just something they do in the classroom.

" They can take these skill sets as life skills to be able to communicate with all people from all cultures and all diverse populations. "

Students at Beverley District High School have been learning Auslan over the past four years. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Students from the school have previously attended the Beverley Frail Aged Lodge where they taught residents everyday signs.

"The children loved it because they were the real experts teaching the older generation," Ms Freeman said.

She said learning Auslan was accessible to all students, with lessons differing from traditional classes.

"'I feel I have the best job in the world because the students are so enthusiastic, they want to learn," Ms Freeman said.

"It's a level playing field so they're not having problems reading or writing or doing maths.

"Everybody can enjoy it and everybody can learn and everybody can have success."

title: Creator's monster Halloween display proves 'people aren't so scary'
text:
With its webs, witches and werewolves, Halloween draws Zoe McKavanagh further out of her shell every year.

The 30-year-old Gold Coast resident lives with autism and has, for the past six years, slowly collected a monster haul of pumpkins, spiders and skulls of different shapes and sizes.

Zoe McKavanagh is considering a competition to name the giant spider, which is her favourite decoration. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"I love Halloween because of how happy it makes everyone," Ms McKavanagh said.

"People often call Christmas the giving holiday but with that you only do family and friends — this way you can do it for everyone."

Speaking with people outside her family hasn't always been easy for Ms McKavanagh.

"I did a lot of her talking for her when she was growing up," her mum and full-time carer, Colleen Millard, said.

"She would whisper in my ear because she was scared of talking to people, she wouldn't go around people, or she would hide from them."

Colleen Millard (left) says her daughter used to hide from the trick-or-treaters who would come to visit their home. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

She said in the first few years of creating Halloween displays, her daughter would do all the work but then hide in the house when trick-or-treaters arrived.

"Slowly, over the years she's started to stay out … and now it's got to the point where she'll talk to people without me doing it for her," Ms Millard said.

" It brings tears to your eyes … that's such a big, big step. "

Despite the ghoulish and often dark themes of Halloween, Ms McKavanagh said she saw light in the community's love of the occasion.

Zoe McKavanagh's collection of pumpkins grows larger after every Halloween. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"Everyone's so nice, they're so excited about the decorations, so kind about the treats and everything," she said.

" It's made me realise that people aren't so scary. "

Retailers use spooks as signpost for spending

Griffith University business analyst and retail expert Graeme Hughes said the national consumer spend on Halloween had increased year-on-year for the past decade.

Research from the National Retail Association and Roy Morgan predicts Australians will spend more than $500 million on Halloween this year.

"If we go back 10 years, very few consumers would celebrate this tradition but now, 10 years on, we're seeing all sorts of people really buying into it," Mr Hughes said.

Some Halloween decorations incorporate movement sensors and electronics, driving up the cost. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

He said once people started spending, retailers were quick to encourage them to keep it up.

"It's critical for business now to signal that something's happening, to get everybody, young and old, involved in that retail spend cycle," he said.

"We know that this really does have a knock-on effect for those Christmas sales … and we're seeing retailers trying to get as much as they can when we know that consumers are doing it tough."

Little rest for the wicked or the whimsical

Halloween display creator Ian Kane draws on his experience as a DJ and lighting technician to put on an annual show in the front yard of his Gold Coast home.

Ian Kane says Halloween allows him to be more creative than he can with Christmas lights. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Mr Kane said he'd been doing a Christmas display for the past 20 years, but first decided to "take on" Halloween five years ago.

"I've always loved Christmas, but I find Halloween's a bit more exciting," Mr Kane said.

" There's a lot more stuff you can do with Halloween, so it makes it more interesting. "

Mr Kane's display incorporates dozens of creepy characters, smoke machines, lasers, lights, and even motion sensors connected to pneumatic relays and an air compressor.

Ian Kane's favourite Halloween decoration is an animatronic dragon to which he's added a smoke machine. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"With all the pneumatics, you can get some really powerful effects and some good jump scares," he said.

"It's just great seeing all the kids happy."

After Halloween, Mr Kane spends days dismantling his display — almost as long as he spends putting it up.

Ian Kane's Burleigh home is transformed every Halloween. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Then his attention turns to his Christmas lights.

"Come Boxing Day I turn everything off for Christmas and then get to have a bit of a break," he said.

"I'll get a week off work if I'm lucky."

title: Council proposes road extension through protected wildlife sanctuary
text:
Since it was established nearly a decade ago, the Wandiyali-Environa Wildlife Sanctuary has become an ecological haven.

It is home to a variety of native plants and animals, many of them rare or endangered.

Box-gum grassy woodland, gang-gang cockatoos and pink-tailed worm lizards are all there, and a koala was sighted earlier this year — a rare species in the ACT region.

Carolyn Larkham opposes council's proposal to build a road through the sanctuary. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

"We've seen an amazing response here," Carolyn Larkham, Wandiyali's environmental coordinator and landowner said.

"We're still getting new sightings of plants and animals … There are these species that we know are regionally very rare, and they're all represented here in this one place."

The natural ecosystem is near the growing Googong and Jerrabomberra region, where residents have hoped for decades for better road infrastructure to connect the area to Canberra and the ACT.

Wandiyali-Environa Wildlife Sanctuary is home to several threatened animals and plants. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council endorsed its preferred road route last week, after ongoing debate and a consultant's report into the various development options.

Known as Option 5, the road will cut through the wildlife sanctuary.

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council Mayor Kenrick Winchester said it was the only viable choice.

Kenrick Winchester says putting the road through the sanctuary is the right choice. (ABC News: Ruby Thomas)

"We will now be proceeding with getting the studies done to try to prove to the New South Wales Minister for Environment that the road must and should only go via that Option 5," he said.

The council's preferred option is more expensive than several others, but the consultant report showed it had a higher cost-benefit ratio.

Ms Larkham said the choice was disappointing, given there were alternative routes available and other recommendations made.

Conservation Council ACT biodiversity working group chair Matt Whitting said he understood residents' commuting needs, but highlighted that there had been 25 years of conservation work at the protected sanctuary.

Matt Whitting is concerned about the future of the sanctuary. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

"We've got a lot of sympathy with the residents of Googong, who've been told for decades that this might be possible and that might be possible," he said.

" But this place has been set aside securely, legally protected, and we can't afford to just keep squandering opportunities to protect really high conservation value places like this one. "

Cr Winchester said council wanted to limit damage to the stewardship site, and it was a "delicate balance between the environment and the needs of the population".

The Queanbeyan-Palerang council will take its case to the New South Wales government. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

He said that all the options for the road route were "problematic", but council would not support a route through existing suburban development.

"The council made it very clear that they do not want the road to impact on houses and on people and where they live," he said.

" We would much prefer to have a small impact on that sanctuary site than potentially have to knock down, compulsorily acquire houses that people have spent generations growing up in. "

The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council will take its case to the New South Wales government.

The government is not expected to decide on the proposal until at least mid-next year.

It is a decision that Ms Larkham said must be made in the interests of the natural environment.

"We have community programs with Jerrabomberra High School and University of Canberra, and we have community engagement through our wildflower walks," she said.

"Habitat fragmentation is such a death of a thousand cuts to these sorts of areas."

title: Etsy cracks down on AI-copying issues but some users still sceptical
text:
Global online marketplace Etsy has updated its artificial intelligence policies following widespread criticism from users faced with AI-generated products.

Etsy recently sent an email to sellers, informing them of the changes, and published the new policy online.

"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," it said.

" AI is threatening [buyer] trust, and we have a responsibility to protect it. "

The statement provided a list of policy updates to set clearer restrictions on AI use.

Lucy Cooper checks out Etsy's new policy on AI-generated art. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

One requires sellers to include at least one unedited photo of their item against a real background, with exceptions for some products.

"Some digital items, like audio files, don't have visual elements. For those listings, you may use representative imagery, including AI-generated images, as long as it doesn't mislead buyers about what they're purchasing," it said.

Photo-editing tools, such as exposure, crop and background adjustments, including AI, are still allowed for other listing images "as long as those edits don't make the item appear different".

Etsy said that if the item received by buyers is "materially different" from the listing images, the seller may be responsible for a refund.

Lucy Cooper is sceptical that the platform is taking AI-generated copies seriously. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Another update banned AI-generated functional guides like recipes and crochet patterns.

Listings for these items that aren't AI-generated must also provide an image of a real result.

New features are also being introduced, such as a specific "misleading AI-generated images" reporting option and guidance for listing photos.

However, at this stage, the reports are only to help Etsy "better understand how members perceive potential AI misuse and won't result in immediate enforcement action".

It's unclear if the guidance for listing photos has been implemented.

AI-generated art, like prints, are still permitted "when sellers play a clear creative role in what they create and are transparent about their process".

'Bit of a laugh', seller says

Earlier this month the ABC spoke with Lucy Cooper, a Hobart-based crochet artist known for her 90s-surf-wear-inspired spiral beanie design.

Ms Cooper said she had discovered an Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her crochet beanie pattern, with AI-generated images.

Lucy Cooper's small business started gaining traction in March with her "spiral beanie" design. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Etsy's new AI policy changes suggest it will prevent experiences like hers from occurring.

However, it has since happened again.

Ms Cooper found another Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her beanie pattern, and all eight product images were generated by AI.

Lucy Cooper has been crocheting since she was 15. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The listing was published on October 28, six days after Etsy announced its policy update.

"It's good that they're actually doing something, but I think that it's a little bit of a laugh," Ms Cooper said.

" They're addressing the problem, but they're not actually really doing anything about it. "

Ms Cooper said she felt the changes relied too heavily on sellers doing the right thing.

"The problem is people aren't being honest," she said.

"If you're the platform owner, you have to do something to make it so that this can't happen."

Lucy Cooper recently discovered a US-based Etsy store was selling a copy of her spiral beanie with AI-generated images. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Etsy's community has mixed feelings

Following Etsy's announcement, users across the globe took to social media to voice their opinions on the changes.

In an Instagram post, Jade, a seamstress, said, "It seemed like [Etsy] didn't want to demonise AI usage, but I think that's going to alienate a large part of their database — buyers and sellers alike — who are truly anti-AI."

In the comments, one user said: "They are trying to serve a larger group of people and shops. Banning AI entirely would mean a lot of shops would close.

"I am a visual and web designer, photographer and … wood artisan. I create physical and digital crafts. There is a place for AI, and banning it would really make some parts of the design process unnecessarily slow.

" Just because so many create AI slop does not mean the entire use of AI should be banned. It just needs more guidance. "

In another post, Molly, a crochet artist, asked, "is Etsy going to take a proactive approach to finding [AI-generated pattern listings]? I think that these are positive changes … I'll believe it when I see it."

Etsy has acknowledged it failed to address AI issues as quickly as users may have wanted. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Some are frustrated by Etsy's decision to not immediately remove listings that are reported for AI misuse.

"I think [the new reporting feature is] really good. But if you're not going to do anything about it, what's the point of it being there?" Ms Cooper said.

"When you report an item, and you say it's AI-generated or this pattern doesn't work or it's copyright or it's plagiarism, it should immediately get taken down, or they should notify you what's happening with it."

Changes just a 'starting point', Etsy says

Etsy says it is aware there is more to address as AI continues to evolve, and that it will keep making improvements as it listens to its community and learns what it needs.

"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," the company said.

"It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business.

"We are closely monitoring developments in this rapidly evolving area, listening to feedback from our community, and periodically re-evaluating our policies.

"These changes are our starting point, not the finish line."

The shape of the Melbourne Cup changed dramatically on Saturday morning after Irish import and expected pace-maker Defiantly failed a vet test. The Joseph O’Brien stayer has set European racing alight in the past six months by adopting daring catch-me-if-you can tactics and was expected to turn Tuesday’s 3200m race at Flemington into a gruelling test of stamina that would suit the Europeans. The Joseph O’Brien-trained Defiantly during a track gallop at Werribee. Getty The five-year-old gelding presented with sensitivity in a hind foot when first inspected at Werribee earlier this week, but the O’Brien stable was quietly hopeful it would come good by the follow-up veterinary examinations today. But Racing Victoria vets were unable to pass it fit to run.

Advertisement

The scratching means that another O’Brien runner, Kizlyar, will make the starting 24. Related Article Victorian racing These horses will win the VRC Derby and Coolmore Stud Stakes In further action taken today, stewards charged trainer Nick Ryan with possessing a prohibited substance and ordering two of his Derby Day runners – Doubt Time and Anglais – to be scratched. Stewards released a statement saying Ryan was allegedly found to have two syringes of Darbepoetin Alfa in the glove box of his car outside his Flemington stables on Saturday morning. Darbepoetin Alfa is a stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone.

Advertisement

The inquiry has been suspended until Monday. Ryan has reserved his plea. Defiantly, purchased by Australian Bloodstock earlier in the year with the Melbourne Cup always its focus, is part-owned by media identities Yvonne Sampson and her husband Chris O’Keefe. Dozens of owners and their friends and families are in Melbourne for the race and are said to be devastated to have come so far, only to be scratched at the 11th hour. Blake Shinn’s Melbourne Cup mount Saint George was scratched from the race on Thursday after failing to pass mandatory pre-race scans. Getty Images Defiantly rocketed into contention in August after a 5.5 length win in the group 2 Prix Kergorlay (3000m) at Deauville in France.

Advertisement

The gelding has already been withdrawn from Melbourne Cup markets. The field will be finalised later today, and the all-important barrier draw will be held at 6.30pm. O’Brien’s racing planner Kevin Blake told this masthead on Friday that stable staff were confident Defiantly would be OK. The horse had passed all leg scans. “It was just a minor bit of sensitivity in a hind foot type of thing that happens all the time,” he said. Blake said Defiantly had “the potential to play a big role” in setting a fast Melbourne Cup tempo. “The way he does things is quite unique,” Blake said.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait “Generally, our staying races would be run at more even or a more solid tempo. I think that would be the concept I’d say pretty universally amongst the internationals.” Today’s scratching followed the withdrawal of the Ciaron Maher-trained stayer Saint George on Thursday after leg scans showed it was at “heightened risk of injury”. Internationals Wine Dark Sea and Enfjaar both passed follow-up vet checks on Saturday morning. Racing Victoria said on Saturday that stewards had concluded the first of two rounds of mandatory pre-race physical veterinary inspections.

“In the opinion of the veterinarians, Defiantly remains unsuitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup and has been withdrawn from the race by order of the stewards acting on veterinary advice,” an RV statement said. “In addition, the veterinarians re-inspected Small Fry (Joseph O’Brien) and in their opinion the horse is no longer suitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup. London: An Australian extreme fitness athlete who soiled herself during a race said she was “traumatised” by the backlash to the incident. Joanna Wietrzyk apologised to her fellow competitors, saying she “didn’t really think about those around me” when she became unwell during the Hyrox event in Beijing in September. The 24-year-old pushed on to win the event and later said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning. Pictures and videos from the competition showed faeces running down Wietrzyk’s legs, on to the mats and communal equipment.

Advertisement

The athlete retroactively withdrew from the race, but organisers faced intense criticism for allowing her to continue despite the potential health risks to other competitors. They insisted that affected lanes were deep-cleaned and contaminated equipment was removed, but Moritz Fürste, Hyrox’s co-founder, apologised and said the company made a mistake by not reacting immediately. New rules have been put in place giving organisers the power to remove athletes if their bodily fluids pose a contamination risk. Australian Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised following the notorious Hyrox incident. Getty Images In an interview with the BBC, Wietrzyk said the backlash she received after the incident was “traumatic”.

Advertisement

“Yes, I did make the wrong decision, but I don’t believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online … At the end of the day, I’m only human,” she said. She added that it had been a “mentally and emotionally taxing period”, with her family also receiving threats online. “[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who’s 24, just out there racing,” she said. The athlete revealed she planned to return to competition but was “nervous” to do so. “I don’t want it to become my identity,” she said. Wietrzyk said that despite suffering from food poisoning she went into the race “feeling fresh, feeling really, really good”.

Advertisement

“It was a very sudden experience,” she said. She had completed two runs and the SkiErg, a machine that simulates skiing, and was midway through the burpee broad jumps exercise when she became unwell. Related Article Fitness ‘I regret the decision’: Hyrox athlete apologises, forfeits event after soiling herself “It wasn’t until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire ... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person … and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing,” she said. “Obviously I did put other people at risk,” she admitted.

“It was my decision to continue racing, so I take full responsibility for that. I didn’t really think about those around me … The decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision, and I’m truly sorry for everyone that I did affect.” Some athletes at the event were refunded their entry fees. In a Hyrox event, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing high-intensity fitness exercises using shared equipment. title: Western Sydney Airport is made for western Sydney. So how does travel there stack up? We tested it
text:
Three reporters travel to the new Western Sydney Airport from western Sydney. What method of travel wins?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With Sydney’s new airport up and running, a key question has lingered amidst the excitement: how does one get there? Armed with fake luggage and a keen eye for bus routes, the Herald’s western Sydney reporters set a challenge to see who could make it to the airport the quickest via public transport for a real flight. Our goal was to arrive the recommended two hours before a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast. In theory, it’s easy: get the metro. But the Western Sydney International Airport metro line is not due to be completed until December 2027 at earliest, so there are currently limited public transport options, in addition to driving. We picked the three largest western Sydney hubs – Parramatta, Penrith and Campbelltown – as the starting points for our journeys. 9am: My plan to get this flight has just changed for a third time. I’d initially wanted to take WSI’s much-advertised $25, 50-minute “super shuttle” bus service that runs direct between Parramatta and the airport. But it’s only running twice a day – and the first service leaves after my flight is meant to take off. Next best option was getting a FlixBus, the infamously cheap European green bus company now operating in Australia. Its website boasted about a $3 ticket for a bus leaving at just the right time. But now it has disappeared from the website.

Advertisement

10.30am: It’s going to take me longer, but I’m getting the train to St Marys to join the dedicated free shuttle bus. The train is empty, and I’ve made a discovery: I thought the FlixBus service had disappeared because it was full, but it turns out the company just cancelled the service for today. 10.55am: St Mary’s train station is incredibly noisy because it’s almost surrounded by a construction site for the new metro station – the one that was meant to be ready by the time the airport opened to connect the rest of Sydney to WSI. It’s not. 11.06am: After heaving my luggage through the main street of St Marys, I arrive at the new WSI shuttle bus stop, which is admittedly not much of a bus stop. Three men are constructing a shelter (which is amusing, considering this airport opening was not exactly a surprise) that has left about two dozen passengers waiting for the bus in the sun. The bus arrives as I pull up and join the queue. It’s free, but you need to tap an Opal card to record passenger numbers. The WSI shuttle bus area at St Marys will be functional -- eventually. Anthony Segaert 11.16am: It turns out that despite this bus being full, I’m the only one with a suitcase. The other people on this bus are here for fun. A group of elderly women tell me they’ve heard the airport is beautiful and want to explore it for fun. Another couple tells me they read in the Herald that there weren’t many food options at the airport, so they considered bringing their own lunch for a visit. 11.20am: We’ve just turned off Mamre Road onto Luddenham Road, and it’s a reminder of how developed this area is yet to be: the bus is hurtling along this narrow two-lane track that is crumbling at the sides. 11.39am: We’re here, at just over the hour mark.

Advertisement

9am: Normally, a trip to the Western Sydney Airport from Penrith would only be about a 25-minute drive for me. It’s convenient and faster than travelling to Sydney Airport in Mascot, which often takes me over an hour. So, while many from Sydney’s east may dread travelling to Badgerys Creek, I’m very excited to do so. Normally. Today, however, I’m catching a bus to the new airport and my expectations for a smooth and quick trip are low. Google Maps tells me it will take me one hour and 11 minutes to arrive. 10.40am: While I’m waiting for my 11.05am bus (I’m very early), another airport bus pulls up at 10.40am. One person gets on. Five minutes before my bus comes two other people who look lost join me. There’s a bit of a language barrier, but they mime a plane landing, and I’m able to figure out they’re also travelling to the airport. They seem excited to see the planes, and it’s a good reminder of how many people have been looking forward to visiting the airport. 11.06am: My bus arrives almost right on time and three other people get on. I put my suitcase on the luggage rack and pick one of the many seats available. No one else has luggage. Exactly six minutes later we make our first stop. If this is how often the bus will be stopping it’s going to be a long journey. I wish I had a coffee. 11.27am: We finally make it onto the Northern Road and start driving away from Penrith and towards the airport. It’s still very quiet with only three other passengers on board. I fear I might fall asleep. One person stands up to get off, and the bus driver gets cranky at him for not getting his Opal card out fast enough. I make sure mine is still in my pocket. Ellie Busby arrives at Western Sydney International Airport – with the shortest journey. Kate Geraghty 11.40am: I’m just under 10 minutes away from the airport and my verdict on the journey so far is: it wasn’t as bad as I expected. The few passengers onboard were quiet, the air conditioning on the bus was working, and the bus didn’t stop at all the places listed on the bus route, which made the trip feel fairly quick. I’ve definitely had worse bus trips. But maybe I’m just used to commuting from Penrith to Sydney Airport and this feels like a walk in the park in comparison.

Advertisement

11.48am: End of the line. The remaining two passengers and I disembark into the very hot sun after what ended up being a 42-minute bus ride. Despite what Google Maps told me, I don’t have to walk 30 minutes to get to the airport from the bus station. It’s a huge relief, and I’m already looking forward to experiencing the airport’s airconditioning. And getting a coffee. 9am: My flight is at 2.10pm, and I don’t like hanging about at the airport for too long, so I figure I need to get there at roughly midday. The 845 bus route arrives at the airport by 12.21pm, which feels close enough. It leaves Campbelltown Mall at 11.18am, so I have time to kill. 11am: I need to be at Hurley Street before Dumaresq Street Bus Stop and it will be a quick five-minute walk. Excellent. Past the Dumaresq Street Cinema (which is offering $9.50 tickets to any movie session, an absolute bargain), I find my bus stop and am dismayed. It has no shelter, I am early, and the sun is sweltering. The sign for the bus from Campbelltown to WSI is the only piece of shade. Mostafa Rachwani 11.18am: After 10 minutes contemplating every detail of the bus stop sign as I hide in its very small shadow, the 845 finally arrives, and I jump on, full of hope and wonder. The bus is essentially empty except for someone in a Mad Mex fast-food chain uniform and a school student sitting in the back playing games on his phone.

Advertisement

I clunkily drag my bag to a seat in the middle of the bus. There are no luggage racks on this bus, so my bags sit neatly next to me on the bus seat. Google Maps tells me this trip will be more than an hour long, so I lean back and lament the lack of a footrest. 11.30am: Despite my reservations, this bus ride has so far been about as smooth as possible. Maybe it is the relatively new roads in Sydney’s far south-west, perhaps it’s this expert bus driver, but there are very few bumps or stops on this route. We stop around Narellan and almost everyone gets off and one man, Daniel Schembri, gets on. He’s wearing an Australian Rugby League jersey, and tells me he’s not actually going to the airport. He’s going to St Mary’s and using the airport route as a “shortcut” through western Sydney. That way more people can use it.” 11.45am: I’ve gotten deathly bored now. We’ve made only two stops, and are flying past mostly green fields. Thankfully the bus is air-conditioned and comfortable, but at this point not much else is happening. I check the route, and it says there is still nearly half an hour left.

title: What happens when Australia’s inflation basket gets reweighted?
text:
in brief The latest CPI data shows inflation accelerating, with transport, housing and food among key drivers.

Experts warn inflation pressures will persist, with Australians urged to ease spending where possible.

Inflation continues to rise, with the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) recording an unexpected spike in September.

According to the ABS' Consumer Price Index (CPI), Australia's annual inflation rate sits at 4.3 per cent — up from 4 per cent in August.

The CPI rose to 0.8 per cent in September, doubling the 0.4 per cent rate recorded in August.

Amongst the largest contributors to rising inflation were housing, which rose 5.2 per cent; alcohol and tobacco, which rose 4.3 per cent; health, which rose 3.7 per cent; and food and non-alcoholic beverages, which rose 3.2 per cent.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Retail Expert at the University of Sydney Business School, Lisa Asher, said the CPI has to "adequately reflect" what people are "actually spending" their money on.

"Some of the key changes or movements that we saw last year and this year focus much more on the increase in food and non-alcoholic beverages, as a larger percentage, as well as health costs and transport," she said.

The largest increase was transport, at 8.7 per cent — with petrol being the main contributor, increasing at a rate of 23.6 per cent.

Transport rose 9.4 per cent from August to September alone.

Asher believes it's due to the conflict in the Middle East and rising oil prices.

What is the CPI?

Head of price statistics at the ABS, Rachael McCririck, said the CPI is "really a measure of inflation" or "price changes in the economy".

"We base it on a representative basket of goods and services for Australian households."

The CPI provides a "sense of the underlying price pressures in the economy" but isn't a good measure for how the cost of living crisis is impacting individual households, McCririck said.

"The CPI is really an aggregate measure that informs policymakers and decision-makers about aggregate trends, it informs things like monetary and fiscal policy settings," she said.

"When we talk about the cost of living, we're really talking about an individual household and what pressures they're facing in their day-to-day lives — so to get a sense of that you have to look at the individual consumption basket."

A knitter and an EV owner, McCririck said her basket would differ from the "average household's basket".

"But the weights that we give to the basket for the CPI are based on the average household experience," she said.

"It's not just a straight comparison to an individual; it's actually a very aggregate measure."

Australia's 'basket' has been reweighed each year since 2018.

McCririck said the reweight is based on the ABS' household expenditure survey.

"We've grown forward the CPI weights by looking ... at how trends in the household expenditure change — we've grown the weight forward each year manually."

The next reweight is scheduled for January 2027. However, the ABS has introduced monthly CPI updates.

McCririck said the organisation is "invested" in having a "frequent indicator of the CPI".

"Prices can move quite rapidly at different points in the economic cycle," she said.

"It's really useful for people to be able to get a sense in real time of how key prices in the economy are evolving and how that might be affecting economic decisions by individuals all across the economy."

Inflationary pressures 'going to persist'

Asher told SBS News that rising inflation is a trend that is likely to continue.

"The wars will continue, which means that fuel prices will continue to be high and that has a flow-on effect on goods, logistics and transport systems — which flows onto anything that's imported," she said.

"Many materials, even if they are locally produced here, will increase."

She said inflationary pressures have seen Australians reduce their spending — a habit she hopes can continue into the Christmas period.

"As we move into the Christmas period, people are worse off now than they were at the beginning of the year with inflation — wage growth hasn't kept up," Asher said.

"Some people will be inclined to still spend at Christmas because they feel obliged to do so. I really think that people should be okay to pull back and not overdo it or put things on credit.

"As we move into next year, it's still going to be incredibly tough. Many of the challenges we're seeing are going to persist."

She said Australians should "spend within their means" as "things are quite uncertain".

"Putting things on credit, you're extending that issue into the future, and you're going to pay a higher interest rate," she said.

"We're still seeing the tightening of spending; the last interest rate rise hurt, but I don't think more will be off the table because of these global issues."

Asher hopes that Australians realise that the cost of living crisis is not a household problem, but the result of a "global issue".

"We've got rising inequality, and it's a global issue. We need a number of reforms in Australia including the prevention of offshore profit without paying adequate tax," she said.

"It's sad that people believe that it has something to do with them when the factors that are going on, like the economic indicators, are not them.

She said it's a "widespread problem".

"The system isn't working for the majority of Australians," she said.

"We need more people to be interested in what positive changes can be made from a regulation perspective, to ensure that the wealth of our nation isn't offshore in tax havens, and that it circulates in our economy."

title: As the world grows more divided, Canada and Europe are betting on each other
text:
In brief The EU and Canada announced a new alliance as both faced growing pressure from the United States.

The agreement deepened cooperation on Ukraine, trade, critical minerals and AI.

The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Saturday, aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of US President Donald Trump's moves to tear up US ties with its old partners.

Canada agreed to contribute to a 90-billion-euro ($142.3 billion) support loan for Ukraine and work more closely with Brussels on anything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence, after a two-day summit in Montreal.

"The world's becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and "the weaponisation of trade."

"Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive," he said after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since Trump's shock return to power.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats.

In Montreal, they sketched out a two-tier partnership that von der Leyen, the European Commission president, stressed was "not against anyone else, but for our common strength."

But the plan was partially overshadowed by an intra-EU squabble over what the new relationship should be called, which led to some mixed messaging at the summit.

Unable to fully join the bloc, Canada would become its first "associate member," von der Leyen, said, doubling down on a term opposed by Germany and a handful of other EU states.

The group had successfully pushed to have the label dropped from a joint summit statement, arguing it doesn't exist in EU treaties and needed defining.

Von der Leyen was, however, backed by Carney who also used the title as he addressed journalists after the talks, adding its "substance" would be determined in the coming months.

In Brussels' view, the term defines the unique partnership the EU has with Canada and entails aligning policies, such as on climate and artificial intelligence, Canada joining some EU programs, and creating a stable governance framework.

Broader alliance

As part of this, Canada will have a more stable presence at the EU table.

Carney will take part in an EU leaders summit in June, and European commissioners and Canadian ministers would hold a separate meeting in the spring, Costa, the European Council president, said.

More broadly, Canada and the EU would form the "nucleus" of a larger "alliance for the future" open to other partners, von der Leyen said.

This "will focus on increasing our collective sovereignty and resilience in areas such as AI, energy, critical minerals, quantum, and beyond," Carney said.

A senior EU official explained a key part of it would be coordinating economic security measures, like tariffs, so that they do not inadvertently harm members of the group.

To kick off work, Brussels and Ottawa signed a digital trade deal and a separate pact allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.

READ MORE EU proposes landmark associate membership for Canada

Canada is rich in rare earths and critical minerals that Europe currently sources mostly from China, but needs massive infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry.

The allies agreed to deepen cooperation on satellite connectivity and navigation and artificial intelligence — a field where they are playing catch-up with the US and China.

They also launched work towards Canada's participation in EU initiatives like the Erasmus program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad, and the Galileo satellite program — an alternative to the American Global Positioning System (GPS).

Europe opened its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers, industry and start-ups.

Finally, Carney said Canada will join the EU's 90-billion-euro support loan for Ukraine with an initial participation of 500 million euros, in what von der Leyen described as "a powerful message" of support to Kyiv.

Brussels has been looking for help to plug gaps in Kyiv's finances, as Russia's war of invasion grinds on.
