title: 'A complex attack': What we know about the largest crypto heist in history
text:
In brief Binance said it was working to contain what may be the biggest crypto theft on record.

Investigators linked the multibillion-dollar hack to a group tied to North Korea.

Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Saturday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around US$6.3 billion ($8.9 billion) in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, with investigators pointing to hackers linked to North Korea.

Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had "high confidence" that the attack was orchestrated by a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor, the same group blamed for the US$1.5 billion ($2.1 billion) theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

Another analytics firm, Elliptic, also attributed the attack to North Korea-linked hackers, according to industry outlet CoinDesk.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for the Seth Rogen comedy film The Interview, which mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach," contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote on X.

The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around US$6.3 billion," four times the amount taken in the Bybit hack, the biggest cyberattack of its kind until now.

Binance warned the figure "may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets."

It said around US$3 billion ($4.2 billion) in affected assets had been frozen.

Customers’ account balances have not been touched, but they cannot move funds off the platform while withdrawals remain suspended.

Binance initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals but later said deposits were unaffected. At about 0900 GMT Friday, it said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours.

READ MORE Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage

Fund freeze

The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorised party to execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.

The unauthorised withdrawals drained Binance's hot wallets — the online wallets the exchange uses to process customer transfers — across several blockchains, according to CoinDesk.

Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses."

Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether, a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT, said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion ($2.2 billion) "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."

Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than US$800 million ($1.1 billion) in USDC.

USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins," or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.

The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not respond to requests for comment.

For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.

The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.

Bitcoin plunged nearly five per cent after the news, falling overnight to around US$76,400 ($108,600), its lowest level since mid-September, before recovering slightly to trade at about US$77,300 ($109,800).

Ethereum dropped nearly six per cent, while BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent.

The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

title: Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage
text:
While the prospect of higher interest rates could leave borrowers with less money to spend, it has come as good news for the Australian dollar.

The Aussie surged above NZ$1.25 this week for the first time in more than 13 years, making holidays across the Tasman more affordable for Australians.

Our currency has gained more than 10 per cent against the New Zealand dollar over the past year, giving Australian travellers greater purchasing power.

Two contrasting economic developments helped drive the latest move.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Wednesday's stronger-than-expected inflation report pushed the market-implied probability of a Melbourne Cup Day interest rate rise by the Reserve Bank of Australia above 80 per cent, supporting the Australian dollar.

Across the Tasman, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by leaving interest rates on hold.

Like Australia, New Zealand is also grappling with inflation above its central bank's target, with annual consumer prices rising 3.7 per cent.

Differences in interest rate expectations between the two countries have helped push the Australian dollar higher, potentially making a New Zealand getaway better value.

Major discounts coming for Australian shoppers

Bigger discounts could be on the way during Black Friday and the Christmas period as many Australian retailers battle for shoppers amid slow sales growth.

The sluggish growth in sales could be a sign that consumers are holding back from spending big during the sales, or that cost of living pressures and the prospect of higher interest rates are weighing on household budgets.

Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell told shareholders at the company's annual general meeting (AGM) this week that four in 10 Australians say they often struggle to make ends meet. The supermarket giant estimates groceries account for 10 per cent of household spending among borrowers.

But that hasn't stopped Woolworths from making what its CEO described as a good start to the financial year, with food sales rising nearly 7 per cent in the three months to September. It's doing better than Coles, which reported slower sales growth over the same period at 3.6 per cent, still topping $10 billion in revenue.

It seems that even in tough times, people have to eat — who would have thought?

Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam told the SBS On the Money podcast that shares in the consumer staples sector have risen about 20 per cent so far this year.

"A lot of companies within there, like Woollies, Coles and even Bega Cheese, are benefiting because these are sectors of the market where people are still going to be spending despite where we are in the economic cycle," Lam said.

For retailers selling more discretionary items, however, the picture isn't as rosy.

This week, Super Retail Group, which owns Rebel, Supercheap Auto, BCF and Macpac, said weaker consumer confidence and pressure on discretionary spending had weighed on its business.

It specifically pointed to higher petrol prices as a factor behind the decline in quarterly like-for-like sales at outdoor retailers BCF and Macpac.

JB Hi-Fi, which also operates The Good Guys and kitchen and bathroom retailer e&s, reported negative comparable sales growth across its Australian businesses.

It highlights the pressures many businesses in the discretionary sector — selling wants rather than needs — are facing in this economic climate.

"I think what this means … is potential discounting from these retailers which is of course going to hit margins," Lam said.

"And that's because higher interest rates mean that there's less discretionary money everyday Australians can spend on."

Even Bunnings, owned by Wesfarmers, has seen sales growth moderate, according to Wesfarmers CEO Rob Scott at the company's AGM.

But he said the group's Kmart business was performing well as shoppers increasingly sought value.

For consumers, that could mean more bargains during Black Friday and Christmas sales, as retailers compete harder for every dollar.

Will you have to pay for Claude and its competitors?

AI chatbot Claude's owner, Anthropic, lodged its prospectus this week as it prepares to list on the US sharemarket.

The filing offered investors a detailed look at the company's extraordinary revenue growth, mounting expenses and the risks associated with developing increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

Among the most serious risks identified were "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such (AI) systems were misused, replicated, weaponized [sic], or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Loftus Peak chief investment officer Alex Pollack told the SBS On the Money podcast that other potentially catastrophic threats already exist, including nuclear and cyber risks.

"But the question you’ve got to ask yourself is, what is the probability of those risks happening?" Pollack said.

But buried among the warnings was another risk with more immediate implications for the millions of people using AI chatbots for free.

Anthropic warned that its marketing strategies, including free trials and free subscription tiers, might fail to deliver sufficient financial benefits.

READ MORE A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry

"If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected."

Could that eventually mean an end to free access?

The prospectus doesn't suggest Anthropic has made such a decision, but it does highlight the financial challenge of offering expensive AI services at no cost.

Anthropic reported revenue of US$16.28 billion ($23.12 billion) in the six months to the end of June 2026, compared with US$1.16 billion ($1.65 billion) in the same period a year earlier.

But that extraordinary growth comes with enormous costs.

The company spent nearly US$9 billion ($12.78 billion) on computing and infrastructure over those six months, accounting for more than half its total operating expenses.

It's a reminder that while AI chatbots might be free for many people today, the technology powering them is anything but cheap.

title: 'Pauline is jumping at shadows': Labor denies it tried to lure One Nation MP David Farley
text:
In brief Labor has insisted there's nothing "unusual" about offering David Farley additional staff, citing his Farrer electorate's size.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation is concerned the government is trying to "exert undue political influence over politicians".

Labor insists it is not trying to woo rookie MP David Farley into defecting from One Nation after offering him a much-prized and highly paid extra staffer.

title: Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies aged 86
text:
In brief Patrick Stewart was an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor before taking the sci-fi roles that made him a household name.

The actor was knighted in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.

Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.

"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," it said.

Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from the 1960s.

But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for Star Trek: The Next Generation — a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s Star Trek — that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Make it so," his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catch phrase, "engage".

It was a role he had debated taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearean, Ian McKellen, advised him to spurn Star Trek and remain in theatre.

Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favourite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several Star Trek films and in the later streaming series Star Trek: Picard that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.

"As the seven seasons of TNG went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show," Stewart told the Guardian in 2022.

Stewart also initially baulked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the X-Men movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.

"I said, 'Look, I know this isn't science fiction, but it's fantasy, and I've done that.' But they persuaded me that it wouldn't be like Star Trek, so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong," Stewart told the Guardian.

He became a critical part of another big-money franchise, starting with the first entry, X-Men, in 2000, followed by several more.

Stewart was born on 13 July, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire.

He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War Two an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart's mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.

As a child, Stewart said, acting became a "safe space" after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare —specifically The Merchant of Venice — during a class when he was 12.

He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.

title: What's really behind the numbers? The COVID legacy that's raising new questions
text:
in brief Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, leading to knock-on effects.

Australia has a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs in NSW, Victoria, SA and the ACT.

Long COVID may have affected fewer people for less time than previously thought new research suggests.

Using refined data collection methods, a team from Stanford University in the United States has found that people suffering from chronic COVID-like symptoms may have been misdiagnosed or the illness overreported.

According to the Australian government, Long COVID is defined as contracting COVID-19 and experiencing symptoms for a period of at least 12 weeks afterwards.

But researchers said no clinical test exists for Long COVID, making it difficult to track its prevalence accurately.

They stress that people who were wrongly assumed to have Long COVID may still have experienced debilitating symptoms that could have been caused by other illnesses.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"These findings indicate that Long COVID may be more similar to other extended post-viral syndromes than many have thought," said co-author Steven Goodman, professor of epidemiology and population health in the Stanford School of Medicine.

The Australian government predicted there would be more than 1.3 million cumulative historical Long COVID cases nationwide by the end of 2023 and suggested between 5-10 per cent of people who contract COVID-19 still have symptoms after three months.

How was the research done?

The Stanford researchers reviewed 4.4 billion health insurance records from more than 244 million Americans and say they found a flaw in previous studies.

Older research compared people who tested positive for COVID-19 with people who were never diagnosed or tested.

The issue is that people who are more likely to test also have more records of various health issues, which can create a biased association between those health issues and COVID-19.

Professor Jure Leskovec, another author of the study, explained these discrepancies may substantially overestimate the range and duration of health effects attributable to COVID-19.

"Our new study design found 98 per cent fewer Long COVID-attributable outcomes between four to 12 months after infection compared with conventional approaches applied in the same dataset," he said.

"This doesn’t mean Long COVID is 98 per cent less common. It means that how we design these studies fundamentally changes which health effects we can reliably attribute to COVID."

READ MORE Researchers discover new clue that helps explain severe COVID-19

By focusing only on patients who tested positive or negative, the researchers believe they have produced a more accurate picture of COVID-19's long-term health effects.

Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News refining our understanding of Long COVID is vital for supporting people with the illness.

"We need to make sure that we continue to look into Long COVID, manage those people, try and find tests and obviously also therapies to try and improve their situation," he said.

Difficulties with diagnoses

No diagnostic test exists for Long COVID, and Griffin explained that the criteria some experts use have shifted over time.

It's suspected there could even be different forms of Long COVID, further complicating both diagnosis and treatment.

"It's a complex constellation of symptoms that can involve pretty much every organ system in the body," Griffin said.

The disease can also manifest differently in people or be confused with other illnesses with similar symptoms.

In the worst case, some patients may have their symptoms dismissed or discounted because there is no reliable test.

"They may see some clinicians who say that they don't have anything wrong with them or that it might be due to something else or perhaps it's psychological and not an actual condition relating to their COVID infection."

Experts warn against losing sight of long COVID

Without a reliable test, some Long COVID cases could be underreported, which could mean inadequate resources are directed toward the condition.

"For a short period of time there were some resources deployed to help address that. But then I think in more recent times, a lot of those have been wound up," Griffin said.

Australia has only a handful of Long COVID clinics run by hospitals or GPs.

Dozens more of these clinics and targeted support programs have been discontinued since the height of the pandemic.

Experts said scientists worldwide will keep improving their understanding of the COVID-19 pandemic, both to better understand its impact and to prepare for future public health emergencies.

"COVID-19 had been one of the worst pandemics we face, but it certainly won't be the last. We can take the opportunity to reflect, see how we can be better prepared, and I guess also continue to manage COVID well," Griffin said.

Scrutinising and refining statistics is therefore part of building population wellbeing and resilience.

Leskovec said: "These results should complement physicians’ clinical assessments, not replace them."

"On the other hand, for data scientists, earlier Long COVID studies might need to be revisited with better controls. Our approach could improve those and future population-health studies."

title: Flattened by trains, targeted by vigilantes. Now, delivery robots face Australia
text:
In brief US firm Serve Robotics has launched self-driving robotic food delivery vehicles in Queensland.

Experts say the coming wave of automation will bring both disruption and benefit.

Australia's first delivery robots have begun their autonomous conquest of the Gold Coast's pavements, with experts saying that they could herald a new era in human-robot relations.

United States-based firm Serve Robotics has partnered with DoorDash to deliver meals on robotic wheels to local residents in Queensland, but the technology still has a long way to go before it becomes commonplace elsewhere in the country.

The robots, which carry takeaway orders on pavements at walking pace, are the same as those used by the company and its competitors in the US. They can access an operations depot at Griffith University.

Japan, Colombia, Germany, and others are also in various stages of rolling out autonomous delivery with other companies; however, the droids have not always been warmly received by residents.

In the US, where resentment towards the construction of data centres and the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence is growing, residents in places like Chicago, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia have filmed themselves attacking the robots.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Retired professor Carolyn Marvin was arrested earlier this month after a campaign of protest in which she deliberately stood in front of the machines to stop them doing their jobs. She said she was concerned that robots could soon replace human workers.

Elsewhere, delivery robots have been seen causing damage and chaos when their programming fails to match up with the environment around them.

There have been reports of broken-down robots blocking pavements, stopping at pedestrian crossings as emergency vehicles try to pass, and even running through glass bus stops.

In one viral incident, a robot was filmed straying onto railway lines before being flattened by an oncoming train.

Australians may hold similarly hostile views about the rise of the machines, given backlash against AI and concerns about data centres.

However, Australia Post's experiments with similar autonomous vehicles in 2017 did not spark major pushback.

Robots must overcome barriers

Professor Michael Milford, director of the QUT Centre for Robotics, told SBS News that an autonomous robotic future is by no means guaranteed.

"There's a number of challenges," Milford said. "There's societal acceptance. There's the perception of hogging precious space on the footpath, getting in people's ways occasionally, occasionally driving into bus shelter windows and all that sort of stuff.

"But ultimately, it's a commercial play by these companies, and there is, as far as I can tell, a very challenging path to being sufficiently profitable."

At present, the use of delivery robots is limited. However, analysts expect to see a spike in their adoption over the coming decade. Research firm Transforma Insight reported last year that 2.1 million could be operating worldwide by 2034.

Customers will be able to opt in or out of the robot delivery program starting on Thursday. Credit: Supplied

Although fears about job replacement by technology are widespread, Milford notes that the current food delivery system has its own issues — and is quite efficient.

Without being able to offer some advantage to hand-delivered takeout through price, speed, or otherwise, Milford said the robots face an uphill battle.

Yet, while challenges remain, there are also benefits, such as the removal of cars from the road.

"A lot of [these issues] come down to not the specific technology but to underlying societal things around capitalism and what people will accept," he said.

"This is sort of the pointy end of it, but a lot of this is true of any new technological development."

Productivity gains give robots advantage

While Serve Robotics' vehicles are currently delivering meals from just a single restaurant — Gnocchi Gnocchi, Southport — more are set to join soon.

DoorDash has said the robots are expected to complement its existing delivery drivers by completing short trips in dense urban environments, while humans continue to do longer, cross-city trips.

Professor Hai Vu, head of the Monash Connected Autonomous Vehicle program, told SBS News that automating aspects of the economy is largely inevitable given the productivity benefits on offer.

His team built Australia's first domestically designed and autonomous food-delivery robot in 2025, which they named ARI. Vu said their approach could solve some of the economic issues facing similar machines at present.

"Our approach is actually quite very different," Vu said, explaining that his machines do all of their computing remotely, rather than inside the vehicle as most others do.

"That enables us to have a very simple and low-cost robot," he said. "You could actually scale up thousands of these robots at a fraction of the cost."

Coming to a town near you?

Delivery robots are not automatically legal to operate in Australia and face a raft of regulatory roadblocks, with local councils at the forefront of how they might be regulated.

Gold Coast City Council has been working actively with technology companies and Griffith University to establish how autonomous robots might work on its streets.

Experts at Swinburne University and Monash are also mapping low-speed urban zones where delivery robots and humans might co-exist peacefully.

Milford said that the issues need to be thought through carefully, but that there is little reason Australia couldn't see more robots on its streets soon.

"If you can walk around [a robot], that's fine. But if you're in a wheelchair, for example, that could be catastrophically bad," he said.

"Technically and economically, there is no reason why you couldn't roll out a Waymo service in Sydney tomorrow," he said, referring to the driverless cars operating in the US.

Legally, NSW prohibits the use of fully autonomous vehicles, but Premier Chris Minns has publicly supported the idea, and Waymo — owned by Alphabet, Google's parent company — appears to be preparing to establish a presence in Australia.

"I would not be surprised at all if there was an announcement from Waymo or one of the other organisations that they're going to roll out trials in Sydney in 2027 or 2028," Milford said.

"Elsewhere, I expect to see gradual, steady expansion of these robo-taxis in a lot of places."

While the rollout may be slow, experts say it is coming. Hai cautioned policymakers that they need to play a more active role in addressing how the nation deals with the autonomous future rushing toward it, in order to both mitigate the impacts and reap the benefits.

"If you want to develop the economy," Hai said, "then you need to have the right incentives and provide the right opportunities for people to capitalise on those incentives."

title: A familiar political crisis could be looming as Israel counts its votes
text:
In brief Israel voted five times in less than four years between 2019 and 2022, as alliances repeatedly fell apart.

Neither side currently has a clear path to a majority - uncomfortable deals and potential deadlock could follow.

Israel has just voted, but the country could face another election within months if its deeply divided political parties fail to negotiate alliances to form a new government.

Israelis know this scenario all too well. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections in less than four years, as coalitions repeatedly struggled to assemble majorities or fell apart once they did.

With around 90 per cent of votes from Wednesday's election counted, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, have enough seats in their coalitions to assemble a majority.

Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 53 seats, while Eisenkot's opposition is set for 48, though these figures may still change. The threshold for a majority is 61.

Meanwhile, two Arab parties — the Joint List and Ra'am — are on course for a historic combined 19 seats, potentially handing them significant influence over who forms the next government. But neither side has expressed willingness to work with them, limiting the Jewish blocs' paths to a majority.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Maybe everybody lost in these elections but the Arab parties. And for the Arab parties, it's unclear that they can make use of their huge success," Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog is now tasked with choosing a leader with the best chance of forming a government, with input from each party.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections," he said after early results arrived, urging parties to keep "an open mind".

Israeli politics is known for its twists, turns and unlikely alliances, and many different scenarios could play out in the weeks to come — including a very real possibility of a stalemate that could take months to resolve.

So what happens if neither side can form a government?

The struggle to govern Israel

No party has ever won enough seats to govern Israel alone, forcing leaders to negotiate alliances with other parties.

Eisenkot faces particularly difficult choices, including the prospect of working with Netanyahu in a unity government, or with Arab parties, both of which he said he would not do.

His bloc includes both right-wing parties and the left-wing Democrats, the only Jewish party open to partnering with Arab-led parties.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has indicated he would support an opposition government to oust Netanyahu without formally joining it, potentially opening the door to a fragile minority government.

But working with Arab parties could cost Eisenkot the support of right-wing allies, leaving him with few straightforward paths to power.

Netanyahu's options for partnerships appear more limited. Neither the Arab parties nor any of those in the opposition bloc have expressed willingness to work with him, though in Israeli politics, it's never wise to say never.

"As they say, politics is the art of the possible. In Israeli politics, it's the art of the unimaginable," Ran Porat, an Israel and Middle East lecturer and analyst at Monash University, told SBS News.

A stalemate could benefit Netanyahu

A prolonged political deadlock could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing him to remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.

That prospect has raised questions about how he might use his powers in the interim, particularly amid speculation over a renewed Israeli attack on Iran.

In the days leading up to the election, Netanyahu called for the overthrow of Iran's government. Media reports, which he denied, suggested senior military officials had pushed back against his plans to strike Iran ahead of the vote.

Following the election, Eisenkot warned Israel's security chiefs against allowing Netanyahu to put his political survival ahead of the national interest.

Porat says another deadlock could also result in lower turnout in a future election, disillusioning voters who turned out in force for this vote.

"The side that is anti-Netanyahu, the Arab sector, and the liberals, will be much less motivated to go and vote after they made this enormous effort this time around and did not reach a victory," he said.

Israel has been here before

In the April 2019 election, Netanyahu's party tied with the Blue and White alliance led by Benny Gantz, both securing 35 seats.

But efforts to form a government failed amid disagreements over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews, triggering another election in September.

That vote also failed to produce a government.

A third election in March 2020 eventually resulted in a unity government between Gantz and Netanyahu who agreed to share the prime ministership on a rotating basis.

That government collapsed after less than a year over a budget dispute, before Gantz could take his turn as leader, prompting a fourth election in March 2021.

That vote produced an unlikely eight-party coalition spanning the political spectrum — including an Arab Islamist party for the first time — bring Netanyahu's premiership to an end.

The government was led initially by the right-wing Naftali Bennett and later the centrist Yair Lapid under a power-sharing agreement. But the coalition struggled to reconcile its ideological differences and lost its majority.

Its collapse saw Lapid take over as caretaker prime minister ahead of a fifth election in November 2022, which returned Netanyahu to power.

Lessons for Eisenkot

Porat says the lessons from the last political crisis "have been internalised [by Eisenkot] quite significantly".

He said the collapse of the previous anti-Netanyahu coalition highlighted the importance of party loyalty over ideology, after several right-wing politicians broke ranks, leading to the breakdown of the government.

"So the first lesson is to get people who are loyal to you, which they did, on Eisenkot's side," he said.

The second lesson, he added, is to avoid addressing how to resolve issues with Palestinians, particularly in the West Bank.

"Because if there's something that all parties disagree about ... is what should be done with the settlements and possibly future annexation or compromise."

That issue is "toxic" for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, he explained, particularly if it ultimately ends up including an Arab party.

Views across such a coalition could range anywhere from calling for an immediate two-state solution to annexing the West Bank.

Eisenkot has been cautious about articulating a long-term vision for Palestinians during his campaign, though he has rejected the prospect of a two-state solution under current conditions while opposing Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank.

Many analysts say it's unlikely, even under a new government, that there will be any significant progress towards territorial compromises with Palestinians in the immediate future.

"Avoid that [issue] at all costs, because that will break down the government," Porat said.

— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse.

title: How a Kylian Mbappé 'dictator' meme prompted a Real Madrid apology to China
text:
In brief French footballer Kylian Mbappé and Real Madrid apologised after comments about Mao Zedong sparked backlash in China.

Chinese broadcasters and sponsors cut ties as outrage over the remarks spread online.

Real Madrid has apologised to China after star striker Kylian Mbappé apparently joked about Mao Zedong in comments that sparked a social media storm and saw Spanish football yanked off state TV.

Mocking former leader Mao is taboo in China, and Mbappé's remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger the country.

In a clip of a video interview with French show The Bridge — since taken down — Mbappé talked about being amused by an internet meme of his face photo-shopped onto "some guy, think he's a Chinese dictator", an apparent reference to Mao.

The fallout was immediate. Chinese beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year's World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé, said on Tuesday it had scrapped its partnership with the player, as did dairy firms Mengniu and Milkground.

CMG, which oversees public broadcaster CCTV, said it had suspended broadcasts of La Liga, the world's second-richest football league after England's Premier League.

On Wednesday, Real Madrid issued a statement saying it "wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any offence caused by the recent remarks of our player Kylian Mbappé".

"The club joins in the public apology issued by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself expressed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people," the 15-time European champions said.

The statement came a day after Mbappé — who was the top scorer in this year's World Cup with 10 goals — issued his own apology, saying: "My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."

Mbappé made the comments while speaking with French show The Bridge. Source: Supplied

Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing on Wednesday: "We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made."

La Liga said on Tuesday it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

Earlier, the Chinese state-run Global Times said in an editorial that it was "not difficult to see that the club's longstanding tolerance of such behaviour has contributed to Mbappé's latest offensive remarks".

Mbappé, 27, continued to face a torrent of criticism from Chinese web users on Wednesday, some of it racist.

"His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated," wrote one user on social media platform Weibo.

Mbappé's original joke about Mao was not reposted — or had been scrubbed — from China's tightly controlled social media.

Drinks company Dongpeng was among the Chinese companies to cut ties with Kylian Mbappé. Source: Getty / Liu Junfeng

Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu had meanwhile frozen Mbappé's account, where he has over a million followers.

The same was done on the Weibo app, with a notice stating that "the user has been banned from following due to violating laws or the Weibo Community Convention".

Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappé-related content on Weibo.

A search by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency on Dior and Hublot's Weibo page with Mbappé's Chinese name produced no results.

'Respect history'

Offline too the Mbappé brand appeared to be under threat.

When AFP visited the Adidas flagship store in Beijing's Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid shirts were available for sale, but none bearing the striker's name.

Chinese state media have previously praised Mbappé as a "footballing sensation" and "talent".

His face is plastered on billboards, on soft drinks and across social media.

Kylian Mbappé had sponsorship deals with several Chinese companies that have scrapped the agreements following the controversy. Source: Getty / Future Publishing

Mbappé is sometimes affectionately referred to as "Guigui", meaning "turtle" in Chinese, for his resemblance to a character from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie.

Other major overseas sports leagues have previously angered China.

China suspended sponsorship deals with the US National Basketball Association while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.

This followed Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey tweeting "Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong", referring to protests the Chinese government called separatist and seditious.

"Respecting the history, culture, social customs and national sentiments of others is a fundamental principle for cross-border interaction, a standard of conduct widely upheld by the international community," the official People's Daily newspaper said in an opinion piece.

The shape of the Melbourne Cup changed dramatically on Saturday morning after Irish import and expected pace-maker Defiantly failed a vet test. The Joseph O’Brien stayer has set European racing alight in the past six months by adopting daring catch-me-if-you can tactics and was expected to turn Tuesday’s 3200m race at Flemington into a gruelling test of stamina that would suit the Europeans. The Joseph O’Brien-trained Defiantly during a track gallop at Werribee. Getty The five-year-old gelding presented with sensitivity in a hind foot when first inspected at Werribee earlier this week, but the O’Brien stable was quietly hopeful it would come good by the follow-up veterinary examinations today. But Racing Victoria vets were unable to pass it fit to run.

Advertisement

The scratching means that another O’Brien runner, Kizlyar, will make the starting 24. Related Article Victorian racing These horses will win the VRC Derby and Coolmore Stud Stakes In further action taken today, stewards charged trainer Nick Ryan with possessing a prohibited substance and ordering two of his Derby Day runners – Doubt Time and Anglais – to be scratched. Stewards released a statement saying Ryan was allegedly found to have two syringes of Darbepoetin Alfa in the glove box of his car outside his Flemington stables on Saturday morning. Darbepoetin Alfa is a stimulating agent that mimics a natural hormone.

Advertisement

The inquiry has been suspended until Monday. Ryan has reserved his plea. Defiantly, purchased by Australian Bloodstock earlier in the year with the Melbourne Cup always its focus, is part-owned by media identities Yvonne Sampson and her husband Chris O’Keefe. Dozens of owners and their friends and families are in Melbourne for the race and are said to be devastated to have come so far, only to be scratched at the 11th hour. Blake Shinn’s Melbourne Cup mount Saint George was scratched from the race on Thursday after failing to pass mandatory pre-race scans. Getty Images Defiantly rocketed into contention in August after a 5.5 length win in the group 2 Prix Kergorlay (3000m) at Deauville in France.

Advertisement

The gelding has already been withdrawn from Melbourne Cup markets. The field will be finalised later today, and the all-important barrier draw will be held at 6.30pm. O’Brien’s racing planner Kevin Blake told this masthead on Friday that stable staff were confident Defiantly would be OK. The horse had passed all leg scans. “It was just a minor bit of sensitivity in a hind foot type of thing that happens all the time,” he said. Blake said Defiantly had “the potential to play a big role” in setting a fast Melbourne Cup tempo. “The way he does things is quite unique,” Blake said.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Leading Melbourne Cup chance ruled out, four runners face a nervous wait “Generally, our staying races would be run at more even or a more solid tempo. I think that would be the concept I’d say pretty universally amongst the internationals.” Today’s scratching followed the withdrawal of the Ciaron Maher-trained stayer Saint George on Thursday after leg scans showed it was at “heightened risk of injury”. Internationals Wine Dark Sea and Enfjaar both passed follow-up vet checks on Saturday morning. Racing Victoria said on Saturday that stewards had concluded the first of two rounds of mandatory pre-race physical veterinary inspections.

“In the opinion of the veterinarians, Defiantly remains unsuitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup and has been withdrawn from the race by order of the stewards acting on veterinary advice,” an RV statement said. “In addition, the veterinarians re-inspected Small Fry (Joseph O’Brien) and in their opinion the horse is no longer suitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup. London: An Australian extreme fitness athlete who soiled herself during a race said she was “traumatised” by the backlash to the incident. Joanna Wietrzyk apologised to her fellow competitors, saying she “didn’t really think about those around me” when she became unwell during the Hyrox event in Beijing in September. The 24-year-old pushed on to win the event and later said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning. Pictures and videos from the competition showed faeces running down Wietrzyk’s legs, on to the mats and communal equipment.

Advertisement

The athlete retroactively withdrew from the race, but organisers faced intense criticism for allowing her to continue despite the potential health risks to other competitors. They insisted that affected lanes were deep-cleaned and contaminated equipment was removed, but Moritz Fürste, Hyrox’s co-founder, apologised and said the company made a mistake by not reacting immediately. New rules have been put in place giving organisers the power to remove athletes if their bodily fluids pose a contamination risk. Australian Joanna Wietrzyk has apologised following the notorious Hyrox incident. Getty Images In an interview with the BBC, Wietrzyk said the backlash she received after the incident was “traumatic”.

Advertisement

“Yes, I did make the wrong decision, but I don’t believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online … At the end of the day, I’m only human,” she said. She added that it had been a “mentally and emotionally taxing period”, with her family also receiving threats online. “[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who’s 24, just out there racing,” she said. The athlete revealed she planned to return to competition but was “nervous” to do so. “I don’t want it to become my identity,” she said. Wietrzyk said that despite suffering from food poisoning she went into the race “feeling fresh, feeling really, really good”.

Advertisement

“It was a very sudden experience,” she said. She had completed two runs and the SkiErg, a machine that simulates skiing, and was midway through the burpee broad jumps exercise when she became unwell. Related Article Fitness ‘I regret the decision’: Hyrox athlete apologises, forfeits event after soiling herself “It wasn’t until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire ... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person … and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing,” she said. “Obviously I did put other people at risk,” she admitted.

“It was my decision to continue racing, so I take full responsibility for that. I didn’t really think about those around me … The decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision, and I’m truly sorry for everyone that I did affect.” Some athletes at the event were refunded their entry fees. In a Hyrox event, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing high-intensity fitness exercises using shared equipment. title: Western Sydney Airport is made for western Sydney. So how does travel there stack up? We tested it
text:
Three reporters travel to the new Western Sydney Airport from western Sydney. What method of travel wins?

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With Sydney’s new airport up and running, a key question has lingered amidst the excitement: how does one get there? Armed with fake luggage and a keen eye for bus routes, the Herald’s western Sydney reporters set a challenge to see who could make it to the airport the quickest via public transport for a real flight. Our goal was to arrive the recommended two hours before a Jetstar flight to the Gold Coast. In theory, it’s easy: get the metro. But the Western Sydney International Airport metro line is not due to be completed until December 2027 at earliest, so there are currently limited public transport options, in addition to driving. We picked the three largest western Sydney hubs – Parramatta, Penrith and Campbelltown – as the starting points for our journeys. 9am: My plan to get this flight has just changed for a third time. I’d initially wanted to take WSI’s much-advertised $25, 50-minute “super shuttle” bus service that runs direct between Parramatta and the airport. But it’s only running twice a day – and the first service leaves after my flight is meant to take off. Next best option was getting a FlixBus, the infamously cheap European green bus company now operating in Australia. Its website boasted about a $3 ticket for a bus leaving at just the right time. But now it has disappeared from the website.

Advertisement

10.30am: It’s going to take me longer, but I’m getting the train to St Marys to join the dedicated free shuttle bus. The train is empty, and I’ve made a discovery: I thought the FlixBus service had disappeared because it was full, but it turns out the company just cancelled the service for today. 10.55am: St Mary’s train station is incredibly noisy because it’s almost surrounded by a construction site for the new metro station – the one that was meant to be ready by the time the airport opened to connect the rest of Sydney to WSI. It’s not. 11.06am: After heaving my luggage through the main street of St Marys, I arrive at the new WSI shuttle bus stop, which is admittedly not much of a bus stop. Three men are constructing a shelter (which is amusing, considering this airport opening was not exactly a surprise) that has left about two dozen passengers waiting for the bus in the sun. The bus arrives as I pull up and join the queue. It’s free, but you need to tap an Opal card to record passenger numbers. The WSI shuttle bus area at St Marys will be functional -- eventually. Anthony Segaert 11.16am: It turns out that despite this bus being full, I’m the only one with a suitcase. The other people on this bus are here for fun. A group of elderly women tell me they’ve heard the airport is beautiful and want to explore it for fun. Another couple tells me they read in the Herald that there weren’t many food options at the airport, so they considered bringing their own lunch for a visit. 11.20am: We’ve just turned off Mamre Road onto Luddenham Road, and it’s a reminder of how developed this area is yet to be: the bus is hurtling along this narrow two-lane track that is crumbling at the sides. 11.39am: We’re here, at just over the hour mark.

Advertisement

9am: Normally, a trip to the Western Sydney Airport from Penrith would only be about a 25-minute drive for me. It’s convenient and faster than travelling to Sydney Airport in Mascot, which often takes me over an hour. So, while many from Sydney’s east may dread travelling to Badgerys Creek, I’m very excited to do so. Normally. Today, however, I’m catching a bus to the new airport and my expectations for a smooth and quick trip are low. Google Maps tells me it will take me one hour and 11 minutes to arrive. 10.40am: While I’m waiting for my 11.05am bus (I’m very early), another airport bus pulls up at 10.40am. One person gets on. Five minutes before my bus comes two other people who look lost join me. There’s a bit of a language barrier, but they mime a plane landing, and I’m able to figure out they’re also travelling to the airport. They seem excited to see the planes, and it’s a good reminder of how many people have been looking forward to visiting the airport. 11.06am: My bus arrives almost right on time and three other people get on. I put my suitcase on the luggage rack and pick one of the many seats available. No one else has luggage. Exactly six minutes later we make our first stop. If this is how often the bus will be stopping it’s going to be a long journey. I wish I had a coffee. 11.27am: We finally make it onto the Northern Road and start driving away from Penrith and towards the airport. It’s still very quiet with only three other passengers on board. I fear I might fall asleep. One person stands up to get off, and the bus driver gets cranky at him for not getting his Opal card out fast enough. I make sure mine is still in my pocket. Ellie Busby arrives at Western Sydney International Airport – with the shortest journey. Kate Geraghty 11.40am: I’m just under 10 minutes away from the airport and my verdict on the journey so far is: it wasn’t as bad as I expected. The few passengers onboard were quiet, the air conditioning on the bus was working, and the bus didn’t stop at all the places listed on the bus route, which made the trip feel fairly quick. I’ve definitely had worse bus trips. But maybe I’m just used to commuting from Penrith to Sydney Airport and this feels like a walk in the park in comparison.

11.48am: End of the line. The remaining two passengers and I disembark into the very hot sun after what ended up being a 42-minute bus ride. Despite what Google Maps told me, I don’t have to walk 30 minutes to get to the airport from the bus station. It’s a huge relief, and I’m already looking forward to experiencing the airport’s airconditioning. And getting a coffee. 9am: My flight is at 2.10pm, and I don’t like hanging about at the airport for too long, so I figure I need to get there at roughly midday. The 845 bus route arrives at the airport by 12.21pm, which feels close enough. It leaves Campbelltown Mall at 11.18am, so I have time to kill. 11am: I need to be at Hurley Street before Dumaresq Street Bus Stop and it will be a quick five-minute walk. Excellent. Past the Dumaresq Street Cinema (which is offering $9.50 tickets to any movie session, an absolute bargain), I find my bus stop and am dismayed. It has no shelter, I am early, and the sun is sweltering. The sign for the bus from Campbelltown to WSI is the only piece of shade. Mostafa Rachwani 11.18am: After 10 minutes contemplating every detail of the bus stop sign as I hide in its very small shadow, the 845 finally arrives, and I jump on, full of hope and wonder. The bus is essentially empty except for someone in a Mad Mex fast-food chain uniform and a school student sitting in the back playing games on his phone.

I clunkily drag my bag to a seat in the middle of the bus. There are no luggage racks on this bus, so my bags sit neatly next to me on the bus seat. Google Maps tells me this trip will be more than an hour long, so I lean back and lament the lack of a footrest. 11.30am: Despite my reservations, this bus ride has so far been about as smooth as possible. Maybe it is the relatively new roads in Sydney’s far south-west, perhaps it’s this expert bus driver, but there are very few bumps or stops on this route. We stop around Narellan and almost everyone gets off and one man, Daniel Schembri, gets on. He’s wearing an Australian Rugby League jersey, and tells me he’s not actually going to the airport. He’s going to St Mary’s and using the airport route as a “shortcut” through western Sydney. Related Article Western Sydney International Construction noise, coffee and boredom: How to spend all day at Western Sydney Airport “It would take me hours to take a bus or train to get from Campbelltown back home to St Mary’s,” he says. “But this route is a shortcut, I just change over at the airport, and I’m on my way.” “It’s a bullshit route though,” Schembri adds. “Because they should do this every ten minutes when there are flights. That way more people can use it.” 11.45am: I’ve gotten deathly bored now. We’ve made only two stops, and are flying past mostly green fields. Thankfully the bus is air-conditioned and comfortable, but at this point not much else is happening. I check the route, and it says there is still nearly half an hour left.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
